4. On 14.12.2014, respondent No.2, being the Senior Upazilla Fishery Officer, Munshigonj, Sadar made a complaint to the Executive Magistrate to the effect that the Supervisor of the petitioner's Factory has violated Section 5(Kha) of the Protection and Coservation of Fish Act, 1950 (shortly the Act, 1950). Accordingly, the Executive Magistrate (respondent No. l) initated the Mobile Court Case took cognizance of the alleged offence and framed a charge against the said Supervisor under Section 5(Kha) of the Act 1950 for storing and possessing 130 KG of fishing net popularly known as current Jal. The accused Supervisor pleaded guilty of the charge and the Executive Magistrate, in exercise of his powers under the Mobile Court Ain, 2009 (shortly the Ain, 2009), passed the impugned order convicting and sentencing the Supervisor to pay a fine of Tk.5,000/- and confiscating the said fishing net under the said section. 

 5. The petitioner claims that there was no allegation of manufacturing of any Current Jal at petitioner's factory nor any evidence was led by the prosecution on that issue. Moreover the Act, 1950 or the Protection and Conservation of Fish Rules, 1985 (shortly the Rules, 1985) made under that Act, or the Ain, 2009 does not empower an Executive Magistrate to put a factory under sealed lock and key and therefore the impugned order is illegal to that extent. 

 9. Mr. Hossain, the learned Advocate, next submits that the petitioner's grievance is with regard to putting the Factory under sealed lock and key, on the ground that neither the Act, 1950 nor the Protection and Conservation of Fish Rules, 1985 made under that Act, 1985 nor the Ain, 2009 empowers an Executive Magistrate to pass such an order in a Mobile Court Case. Mr. Hossain, the learned Advocate, lastly submits that the unlawful action of the Executive Magistrate is violative of petitioner's fundamental rights with regard to his lawful profession and the related property and that the order has caused serious financial loss to the petitioner and rendered the livelihood of the workers at serious risk and therefore the Rule should be made absolute along with a direction to immediately unseal and to open the factory. 

 The learned DAG next submits that although the Act, 1950 or the Rules, 1985 or the Ain, 2009 does not directly empower an Executive Magistrate to put a Factory under sealed lock and key, this action is justified for the prevention of probable future offences. 

 It is evident that this impugned order covers 5(five) aspects, namely-(1) the conviction and sentence imposed under Section 5(kha) of the Act, 1950, (2) confiscation of 130 KGB of monofi lament current Jai, (3) a direction to deposit the fine in the Treasury, (4) destruction of the confiscated goods by burning and (5) putting the factory under sealed lock and key (প্রতিষ্ঠানটি সিলগালা করা হইল). 

 12. The Rule nisi issued in this case relates to the 5th aspects of the order, namely puttin the factory under sealed lock and key. On this aspect, respondent No.2 has indirectly admitted the absence of the any legal provision in the Mobile Court Ain, 2009 or in the Act, 1950, or in the Rules, 1985 made under the Act, 1950. However respondent No.2 has pleaded that the process of amendment of the Rules, 1985 is in progress. 

 13. In considering the legality of the impugned action taken by the Executive Magistrate we have considered the scheme of the Ain, 2009 and the Act, 1950. The relevant provisions of these two laws ar. briefly discussed below. 

 Section 6(1) of the Ain, 2009 empowers an Executive Magistrate or a District Magistrate to take cognizance of an offence under 97 laws enumerated in the schedule to the Ain, 2009, including the Act, 1950 (vide serial No.24).

 So, in putting the factory under sealed lock and key in terms of the impugned order, Respondent No.1 has clearly exceeded the lawful authority under the Act, 1950 and the Ain, 2009 and the Rules, 1985. Simple because these laws are totally silent about such authority of a Magistrate or other functionaries. 

 (a) The proposed Rules being a delegated legislation must be consistent with the principal legislation being the Act, 1950. 

 (b) In incorporating any provision whether in the Rules, 1985 or in the Act, 1950 or the Ain, 2009, the Respondents should, at the minimum, consider the probable consequences of putting a factory under sealed lock and key e.g. the custody of the property and the period thereof, the manner of handling the property during such custody, the violation of sealing etc and other related matters, keeping in view of the relevant provisions of the Constitution, particularly Articles 40 and 42.
